what_its_for: Promethazine is used to treat nausea and vomiting (such as from motion sickness or after surgery), allergies (like hay fever, hives, or itching), and to help you feel calm and sleepy before or after a medical procedure. It may also be used with other pain medicines to help manage pain.
how_to_take: Promethazine comes as a tablet, liquid syrup, or rectal suppository. Take the tablet or liquid by mouth with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. For the suppository form, insert it into your rectum as directed. Do not crush or chew the tablets — swallow them whole. Use the measuring device that comes with the liquid — do not use a regular kitchen spoon, as it may give you the wrong amount.
dosing: Your dose will depend on what you are being treated for and your age. For adults, the usual dose for nausea is 12.5 to 25 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. For allergies, it is typically 25 mg at bedtime or 12.5 mg before meals and at bedtime. Always follow exactly what your doctor or pharmacist tells you. Never take more than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you are taking promethazine on a regular schedule and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store promethazine tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep suppositories in the refrigerator. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine properly — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking promethazine — it can make drowsiness and dizziness much worse. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert and focused until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking other medicines that cause drowsiness, such as sleeping pills, anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or certain antihistamines, unless your doctor says it is okay. Try to avoid getting too much sun exposure, as promethazine can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath; uncontrollable muscle movements, stiffness, or tremors; severe drowsiness or you cannot be woken up; seizures; fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat; severe dizziness or fainting; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); confusion or unusual behavior; or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat. Also contact your doctor if you feel this medicine is not working for your condition.
when_it_works: Promethazine usually starts working within 20 minutes when taken by mouth. When used as a suppository, it may take a little longer. The effects can last for 4 to 6 hours. If you are using it for motion sickness, it works best when taken 30 to 60 minutes before travel.
special_populations: Children: Promethazine should NOT be given to children under 2 years of age because it can cause serious breathing problems that may be life-threatening. Use with caution in children older than 2 years and only under a doctor's guidance. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to the drowsiness and dizziness caused by this medicine and may have a higher risk of falls. Use the lowest effective dose and talk to your doctor about safer alternatives if needed. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using promethazine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It may be used for nausea during pregnancy under medical supervision, but should be avoided close to delivery. Breastfeeding: It is not known if promethazine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Kidney or liver problems: Let your doctor know if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
